passages.t: Keilah saved, and a warning from the ephod
passages.happening:
David hears that the Philistines are attacking Keilah and looting the threshing floors. He asks the LORD whether he should attack them, and the LORD says, “Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah” (verse 2). His men are afraid. They are frightened enough in Judah, let alone at Keilah facing Philistine armies (verse 3). David asks again, and the LORD answers, “Go at once to Keilah, for I will deliver the Philistines into your hand” (verse 4). So David and his men fight the Philistines and save the people of Keilah (verse 5).

Abiathar the priest has come to David with the ephod (verse 6).

Saul hears that David is in Keilah and thinks he has him: ‘for he has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars’ (verse 7). He calls up his army (verse 8). David tells Abiathar to bring the ephod and asks the LORD two questions. Will Saul come? “He will,” said the LORD. Will the people of Keilah hand David over to Saul? “They will,” said the LORD (verses 10-12).

So David and his men, about six hundred, leave Keilah and keep moving. When Saul hears that David has escaped, he does not go (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
In the last chapter Abiathar, the one survivor of Nob, came to David. Now it is clear why that mattered. David has the ephod, the means of asking God's guidance, and he uses it again and again. Saul, who killed the priests, has cut himself off from it.

Keilah was a walled town in the lowlands of Judah, a few miles south of Adullam, near the Philistine border. The Philistines raided such towns at harvest, when the grain lay on the threshing floors. The threshing floor was an open, flat place, often on high ground to catch the wind, and at harvest a whole year's food lay there in the open.

David acts like a king already. He defends an Israelite town against the Philistines, the very task Saul was anointed to do.

Asking God through the ephod usually took the form of questions with a yes or no answer, one at a time, each with a short reply. David's questions in verses 10 to 12 follow that pattern.

A walled town with gates and bars kept out raiders, but in a siege it became a trap. That is why Saul thinks David has shut himself in. And the people David has just rescued would hand him over.

The verb to ask is the root of Saul's name. The king Israel asked for no longer asks God. David does.
passages.later: As king, David kept this habit of asking before he fought. Before another battle with the Philistines he asked God whether to go up, and the LORD answered, ‘for I will deliver them into your hand’ (1 Chronicles 14:10).
passages.hard:
God said that Saul would come and that the people of Keilah would hand David over, but neither happened. How can God's answers be true if the events never took place?

The LORD's answers describe what would have happened if David had stayed in Keilah. David left, so Saul did not come, and the people never had the chance to betray him. Christians have discussed passages like this for centuries, because they seem to show God knowing what free people would do in conditions that never come about.

Some, often called Molinists after the sixteenth-century Jesuit Luis de Molina, see here evidence that God knows such conditional possibilities and uses that knowledge in guiding events. Others, including many Reformed and Thomist theologians, explain it differently, holding that God knows all things through his own decree and understanding, not through a separate kind of knowledge. Some open theists read the answers as God's accurate reading of present intentions. These are debates among Christians that do not divide the faith.

The chapter's plain teaching is that God knew the danger David could not see, and warned him in time.
passages.asks: David asked God before he acted, and asked again when his men were afraid. Ask whether you bring your decisions to God before you make them, or only afterward. And ask how you respond when the people you have helped would not stand by you.

passages.t: Jonathan strengthens David's hand in God
passages.happening:
David stays in the wilderness strongholds and the hill country of the Wilderness of Ziph. ‘Day after day Saul searched for him, but God would not deliver David into his hand’ (verse 14).

At Horesh in the Wilderness of Ziph, David sees that Saul has come out to take his life (verse 15). ‘And Saul’s son Jonathan came to David in Horesh and strengthened his hand in God’ (verse 16).

“Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will never lay a hand on you. And you will be king over Israel, and I will be your second-in-command. Even my father Saul knows this is true” (verse 17).

The two of them make a covenant before the LORD. David stays at Horesh, and Jonathan goes home (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Ziph lay in the dry hill country south of Hebron, at the edge of the wilderness of Judah: rough ground, caves and few settlements, good country for hiding.

The word hand runs through this chapter. The LORD will give the Philistines into David's hand. Saul thinks God has given David into his hand. The people of Keilah would give David into Saul's hand. And the narrator says plainly that God would not give David into Saul's hand.

Jonathan's visit sits at the center of the chapter, a moment of rest between two betrayals. He strengthens David's hand in God. That does not mean making David feel better. It means pointing him to God's promise that he will be king. The strength comes from God, not from the friend.

Jonathan says openly what his father will not admit: David will be king, and Jonathan will stand beside him. It is a hope that will not come true for Jonathan. This is the last time the two friends meet. The next time Jonathan appears, it will be in the report of his death.
passages.later: The wisdom of Ecclesiastes knows the worth of such a friend: “For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up; but pity the one who falls without another to help him up!” (Ecclesiastes 4:10).
passages.asks: Jonathan did not try to cheer David up. He strengthened his hand in God. Ask who has done that for you, and whom you could visit in their wilderness to do the same. And ask whether you can be glad, as Jonathan was, of a future that does not center on you.

passages.t: Betrayed by the Ziphites, and the rock of escape
passages.happening:
The people of Ziph go to Saul at Gibeah and tell him where David is hiding, ‘in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah south of Jeshimon’ (verse 19). They promise to hand him over (verse 20).

Saul answers warmly, praising them because ‘you have had compassion on me’ (verse 21). He sends them back to find out exactly where David hides, for he has heard that David is very cunning (verses 22-23).

David and his men are in the Wilderness of Maon. Saul comes after him, and David goes down to the rock (verses 24-25). ‘Saul was proceeding along one side of the mountain, and David and his men along the other side’ (verse 26). Saul's men are closing in.

Then a messenger comes to Saul. “Come quickly, for the Philistines have raided the land!” (verse 27). Saul breaks off the chase and goes to meet the Philistines. That is why the place is called Sela-hammahlekoth (verse 28). David goes up to live in the strongholds of En-gedi (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The people of Ziph were of the tribe of Judah, David's own tribe. Their willingness to hand him over shows that tribal loyalty was no guarantee of safety.

Saul's warm words to the informers, and his complaint that no one has shown him compassion, reveal how alone and self-pitying he has become. He praises people for betraying the man who killed Goliath for him.

Jeshimon, meaning wasteland, probably means the bare slopes that run down toward the Dead Sea. The name Sela-hammahlekoth is usually explained as the rock of parting, or the rock of escape, remembering how Saul and David were parted just as Saul was closing in. En-gedi was an oasis with springs on the western shore of the Dead Sea, surrounded by cliffs and caves.

The last scene is told with rising tension: Saul on one side of the mountain, David on the other, the gap closing. Then the rescue comes suddenly, from an unexpected direction, a Philistine raid. ‘God would not deliver David into his hand’ (verse 14).
passages.later:
The heading of Psalm 54 sets that psalm here: ‘A Maskil of David. When the Ziphites went to Saul’ (Psalm 54:1). The psalm prays, “Save me, O God, by Your name, and vindicate me by Your might!” (Psalm 54:1).

Psalm 63 is headed ‘A Psalm of David, when he was in the Wilderness of Judah’, and begins, ‘O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You’ (Psalm 63:1). David was in that wilderness more than once, and the heading does not say when.
passages.asks: Saul and David were on two sides of one mountain, and the gap was closing. Ask whether you have known a moment like that, and how it ended. And ask whether you, like the Ziphites, have ever handed over someone who trusted you, to win favor with the powerful.
